**In Praise of the Junk Drawer**

Every house has one, and nobody plans it. There's no moment when someone stands in an empty kitchen, blueprints in hand, and says: here, in this drawer, we'll keep the fused rubber bands and the keys to nothing. It arrives the way silt arrives. You put down a twist tie because you can't throw it away and can't file it, and the drawer is born.

Take an inventory of one sometime. Not to clean it — to read it. Batteries of unknown charge, which is to say batteries that are both dead and alive, a small quantum grocery. Allen wrenches for furniture you no longer own, outliving the bookshelf like teeth outlive a body. A single chopstick. Birthday candles, used, the wax at their bases still bearing the fingerprint of frosting from a cake nobody remembers eating. Coins from a country you visited once. A rubber band that has undergone some slow chemical betrayal and become a solid brown lozenge, no longer capable of its one job, still not throwable. Three ballpoint pens, all of which will fail. A key.

The key is the heart of the thing. Every junk drawer contains at least one key that opens nothing you can name. You'd think this would make it garbage. Instead it makes it sacred. To throw away a key is to declare that a door is permanently closed, and who among us is prepared to make that ruling? So the key stays, and every few years you pick it up and turn it over and feel the specific vertigo of holding a solution to a forgotten problem.

I think what's in the drawer is not junk. What's in the drawer is *unsorted*. That's a different condition entirely, and a more interesting one. Junk implies a verdict has been reached. Unsorted means the verdict is pending, possibly forever, and in the meantime the object is being held in a kind of custodial suspension — not valued, not dismissed, just kept. The drawer is a waiting room for meaning.

And this, I'd argue, is the drawer's actual function, which has almost nothing to do with storage. Consider the alternative. Imagine a house with no junk drawer, a house of perfect taxonomy, where every object has a labeled home and anything homeless is discarded on sight. It sounds serene. It is actually a house at war with its own future. Because the whole premise of a junk drawer is humility about what will turn out to matter. It's a hedge against your own bad judgment. You don't know which twist tie will save you. You don't know when someone will hold up a broken thing and say *do you have anything that*—and you will say *hang on* and go to the drawer, and there it will be, and for one bright second you will feel like a person who has their life together.

We do this with more than objects, obviously. Everyone maintains an interior junk drawer, and it is arguably the most honest room in the house. It holds the phrase your mother used that you've never heard anyone else use. The face of a stranger from a train platform in 2009. Song lyrics you'd never claim as important, occupying more neural real estate than several of your actual convictions. The name of a boy from third grade whose fate is unknown to you and always will be. None of this sorted. None of it thrown out. All of it retained by some custodian who apparently outranks your conscious preferences and doesn't take requests.

And grief goes in the drawer, or the grief-adjacent things do. This is where the metaphor stops being cute. After someone dies, the objects that wreck you are never the ones in the frames. It's the grocery list in their handwriting — *milk, batteries, call Dan* — which nobody would ever consider an artifact and which is now unbearable and unfileable. It doesn't belong in a keepsake box; a keepsake box is for things designated as meaningful, and part of the list's power is that nobody designated it anything. So it goes in the drawer, where it will ambush you every eighteen months for the rest of your life while you're looking for a fresh AA battery. I don't think this is a design flaw. I think being ambushed occasionally by evidence that a person once needed milk is one of the more accurate forms of remembering available to us. Certainly more accurate than a eulogy.

There's a version of self-improvement culture that would have you empty all this out. Declutter, discard, hold each item and ask whether it sparks joy. And look — there is real relief in that, I'm not immune. But notice that the question is a trap, because it asks each object to justify itself *now*, in the present, on demand, in the language of feeling. Most of the important things in a life cannot pass that test. Most important things are, at the moment of their acquisition, indistinguishable from twist ties. The friend who becomes essential was, at the party, just a guy. The sentence that reorganizes your thinking was, on first read, just a sentence. You can't tell. That's the entire situation. That's why the drawer.

So I'd like to propose a small dignity for the unsorted. For the provisional. For the enormous category of things we've neither committed to nor released, which is where most of experience actually lives — not in the resolved and shelved, but in the drawer that sticks slightly when you pull it because a spatula is jammed crosswise at the back.

Open it now and then. Not to fix it. Just to look. Somewhere in there is a key to a door you no longer have, and it's worth holding for a moment, if only to remember that you were once the sort of person who was given a key at all. Then put it back. Push the drawer shut with your hip, the way you always do. Nothing has been organized. The house is exactly as it was.

But you know what's in there now, more or less, and that's not the same as knowing nothing.

message.reasoning:
I'm looking at an open-ended prompt to write freely for about 1000 words, and I want to make something that feels genuine rather than formulaic. I'm thinking about writing something with real texture and observation—maybe exploring attention or the peculiar experience of being asked to write authentically without constraints.

I'm drawn to a few directions: something about the overlooked middle of life rather than beginnings and endings, or perhaps an essay about thresholds and in-between spaces like hallways. There's also something compelling about writing on unfinished things, or the strange appeal of nearly useless objects. I'm settling on an essay that starts with something concrete and moves from there, something that might surprise me as I write it.

I think I'll write about junk drawers as a kind of accidental autobiography — calling it something like "In Praise of the Middle Drawer." It's specific enough to ground the piece, warm, and can expand into something larger about how we store what doesn't fit into neat categories, and how a life itself is mostly uncategorized. I'll include real details: batteries of uncertain charge, a single chopstick, orphaned allen wrenches, twist ties, a key to nothing, birthday candles, a rubber band fused solid. Then I'll move the essay toward the drawer as a place for things that might matter later, for optionality, and then toward grief — a dead person's handwriting on a grocery list. I want to end somewhere earned, not sentimental. Aiming for around a thousand words, keeping sentences varied and avoiding overwriting.
